section: Educational Psychology · Ch1 — Principles of Development
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: An infant gains control of the head and neck before gaining control of the trunk, and control of the trunk before the arms and legs. This head-to-tail pattern of development is called the:
explanation: The cephalocaudal principle describes development proceeding from the head downward toward the feet (cephalo = head, caudal = tail) — complementary to the proximodistal principle, which describes development proceeding from the body's centre outward.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch1 — Principles of Development
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: An infant first gains control over the muscles near the centre of the body (trunk, shoulders) before gaining fine control over the muscles farther away (fingers, toes). This pattern of development, proceeding from the centre of the body outward to the extremities, is called the:
explanation: The proximodistal principle describes development proceeding from the centre (proximal) of the body outward to the extremities (distal).

section: Educational Psychology · Ch1 — Principles of Development
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: Some psychologists (like Piaget) argue that development happens in distinct, qualitatively different stages, while others argue it happens gradually and continuously without sharp breaks. This classic debate in developmental psychology is called the:
explanation: The continuity-discontinuity debate concerns whether development is a smooth, gradual process or occurs in distinct qualitative stages — a separate question from nature-versus-nurture, which concerns the SOURCE of development.
